## Introduction  {.unnumbered}

In this problem set, you will use a variety of _linear_ and _non-linear_
regression methods on both a 'tall' and a 'wide' prediction task. As you 
work through these, be sure to consider the relative pros and cons of each
approach. As we've emphasized throughout the semester, there is no 
universally best method -- "no free lunch" -- for any given task and the best
method for a task will be a complex function of data types, your goals, data 
size, and personal preferences. 

## Data Files  {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
dc_bike <- read_csv("problem_sets/data/ps02_dc_bike.csv")
ca_drought <- read_csv("problem_sets/data/ps02_ca_drought.csv")
```


We introduce two new regression data sets for this problem set. The first, 
the [DC BikeShare](./data/ps02_dc_bike.csv) data set, has hourly bike-rental 
counts from the [Capital Bikeshare](https://capitalbikeshare.com/) program 
serving Washington, D.C.[^citi] This data contains `r NROW(dc_bike)` rows of 
hourly data (`r min(dc_bike$time)` to `r max(dc_bike$time)`) and your goal is 
to predict the number of bikes rented (checkout time) in
that hour. To predict ridership, I provide you local temperature, humidity, 
wind speed, precipitation as well as some pre-constructed time features
(hour 0 to 23), day of week, day of year, and weekend / weekday. You can 
choose to make your predictions on a linear (`ridership`) or logarithmic
(`log_ridership`) scale, but you can only use one `ridership` variable. 

```{r}
#| eval: false
dc_bike <- read_csv("https://michael-weylandt/STAT3106/problem_sets/data/ps02_dc_bike.csv")
skimr::skim(dc_bike)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
skimr::skim(dc_bike)
```

This is the "tall" data set referenced below. 

The second "wide" data set arises from an important problem in climate 
forecasting. Specifically, in the [CA PDSI](./data/ps02_ca_drought.csv) data set, 
we have global sea surface temperatures (`sst`) and want
to use them to predict the degree of drought in California. (Think *El Nino*.)
This data set has `r NROW(ca_drought)` rows of historical monthly data (via
NASA's POWER data) along with `sst` from a
roughly 4 degree global grid, which can be used to predict the 
[Palmer Drought Severity Index (PSDI)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palmer_drought_index)
for California in the same month.[^land]

```{r}
#| eval: false
ca_drought <- readr::read_csv("https://michael-weylandt/STAT3106/problem_sets/data/ps02_ca_drought.csv")
skimr::skim(ca_drought)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
ca_drought |> select(1:10) |> skimr::skim()
```

(Many similar rows omitted)

[^land]: Note that we only have 
`r ca_drought |> select(starts_with("sst")) |> NCOL()` SST columns, even though
we're on a 4 degree grid (4050 total cells) because we have to mask out cells
with land.

[^citi]: Capital Bikeshare operates quite similarly to NYC's CitiBike program. 


## ML Best Practices Question (16 Points)

Consider the scenario below in I describe a hypothetical application of
ML. There are (at least) 5 issues in how the ML system is developed, tested, 
and deployed. Identify **four** distinct issues and, for each issue you identify,
describe: 

- The mistake that was made (1 points)
- The likely adverse impact arising from the mistake (1 points)
- What should have been done instead (2 points)

(This is what lawyers might call an "Issue Spotter" question.)

**Scenario**: Hamilton, Butler, and Low (HBL) is an elite management consulting
firm, which has long-prided itself on hiring only the most elite and high-achiving
Ivy League undergraduates. To be more 'AI forward', to reduce historical
hiring biases, to eliminate the thousands of (otherwise billable) partner hours 
spent vetting undergraduate applications, HBL tasked its People Analytics team
with developing an automated screening engine dubbed *Project ROAR 
(Rapid Objective Applicant Ranking)*. 

Historically, HBL's recruitment had relied heavily on informal alumni 
networking, on-campus partner dinners, and unstructured behavioral interviews, 
which leadership acknowledged had favored traditional feeder networks and a 
predominantly male candidate pool. To cast a wider, more meritocratic net, the 
project sponsor announced that ROAR would serve as an automated, 
interview-free gatekeeper for all incoming applicants: any candidate whose 
predicted first-year job performance score exceeded 78 on HBL's standard 
continuous 1 to 100 rating scale would automatically receive an offer for a 
final-round interview slot, while those below 78 would be rejected without 
additional human review.

The analytics team began by querying internal HR records from 2017 to 2021, 
compiling complete digital application files and subsequent first-year review 
scores for 1,400 junior associates hired under the firm's historical recruiting
regime. To capture every possible objective signal, the data engineers extracted
hundreds of resume keywords, collegiate club memberships, undergraduate major
indicators, and assigned onboarding salary tiers, while imputing missing 
collegiate transcript grades with the global mean across the entire 5-year
archive. Before fitting any models, the team normalized all continuous predictors
using the mean and variance computed over the complete 1,400-employee database,
and ran a univariate screening step across all columns to pre-filter down to
the top 200 most correlated features. They adopted Mean Squared Error (MSE) as
their primary accuracy measure, reasoning that quadratic penalties on score 
discrepancies were mathematically tractable, captured the 'big miss is a big loss'
phenomenon in hiring, and cleanly mirrored standard regression theory. 

For the predictive engine, the team evaluated high-dimensional linear models and
forward stepwise polynomial regression. To tune the model, the lead 
analyst configured the forward stepwise algorithm to continually add polynomial 
terms and pairwise interactions until the in-sample Residual Sum of Squares (RSS)
ceased to drop by more than 0.25%, celebrating when the model achieved an 
in-sample $R^2$ of 0.91. When fitting Ridge and Lasso models as benchmarks, the 
engineers selected the penalty parameter $\lambda$ that maximized in-sample 
explained variance on the training set, concluding that because $\lambda \to 0$
delivered the lowest error, regularization was unhelpful and could be safely
omitted. To evaluate the pipeline prior to deployment, the team partitioned
the 1,400 past employees into an 80/20 train/validation split using uniform
random sampling across the rows. Upon finding that the model achieved a
validation RMSE of just 3.4 points on the 1–100 scale, the team declared ROAR 
production-ready.

The system was launched for the 2024–2025 recruiting cycle, where HBL actively
marketed its new "resume-blind, network-free" process to hundreds of 
non-traditional campuses, successfully attracting an applicant pool that was
majority female and demographically unprecedented for the firm.

4. When performing many statistical tests (or equivalently, when estimating many
   different model parameters) issues of _multiple testing_ come to the fore. 
   As discussed in class, one way we can address this is by examining the 
   _false discovery rate_ instead of the _false positive rate_ of our tests. 
   Define the FDR mathematically, provide an intuitive interpretation, and explain
   why it may be preferred over traditional false-positive rate control. (3 points)

## First-Order Methods (15 Points)

In this question, you will apply _first-order_ (gradient-based optimization) 
methods to linear models. You will compare 'classic' gradient descent with
stochastic accelerated variants and see the benefits of early stopping. 

### Gradient Descent for Linear Models (5 Points)

When faced with a very large data set, it may be computationally impractical to 
use the closed-form solutions to fit OLS or ridge regression. Using the 
[NYSED data](./data/ps01_nysed.csv) from [the previous problem set](./ps01.qmd),
implement a standard *gradient descent* method to fit OLS to this problem (after
performing suitable encoding of categorical variables).  

You may use a fixed (small) step size or, if you are feeling ambitious / impatient,
a _backtracking_ method to select good step-sizes. (See Algorithm 9.2 of the
book by Boyd and Vandeberghe for a simple backtracking method.)

Compare your results against the exact OLS solutions you obtained in the previous
homework. (They will not be _exactly_ the same, but they should be 'close'
in some suitable sense.)

**Use PyTorch, JAX, or similar to compute the gradient of the OLS loss. You
do not need to do this by hand. You should write the implement GD steps out 
directly instead of using a built-in optimizer.**

*Note*: This data set is not actually so large that OLS is actually impractical 
(as you surely saw in the previous assignment). This gives us a nice 
'gold standard' to compare against. 

### Advanced SGD for Linear Models (5 Points)

Pure GD is rarely used for large-scale machine learning as: 

- Computing the ERM loss and its gradient across _all_ training points can be slow
- Tuning step sizes is a bit of a chore

Instead, _stochastic_ (mini-batch) gradient descent and its various 'smart step
size' variants are commonly used. Compare your pure GD implementation from
the previous section against one or more 'advanced' SGD variants (AdaGrad, AdaM,
AdamW, *etc*). Make sure to compare both the quality of the final solution and
the time required to reach that solution and explain your findings.[^time]

For this problem, you may use 'built-in' optimizers and do not need to implement
the SGD methods directly. Continue to use your direct GD implementation from
the previous subsection. 

[^time]: You should look at both _iterations_ (number of steps) and _wall clock
time_ (actual time, in seconds or minutes). 

### Early Stopping of First Order Methods

When fitting first-order methods, it is typically not necessary to run things
'all the way to the end'. Getting the first several decimal places is usually
enough: the final decimal places exist 'within the noise' and give
functionally equivalent predictions. (Put another way, the steps required to
get the 7th digit of precision are functionally pointless and don't typically
improve predictions by a measurable amount.) This motivates _early-stopping_:
the idea that we can stop a first-order method when its predictions stop
improving, rather than running until the weights fully stabilize. 

To implement early-stopping in practice, it is important to have a hold-out 
(validation) set. After each (S)GD update, prediction error on the hold-out set
is computed. When it stops decreasing (or, heaven forbid, starts increasing!), we
stop the first-order method. 

Adapt your GD and SGD methods to implement this type of early stopping. To do
so: 

1) Split your data into 'training' and 'validation' components
2) Modify your update loop to compute the training and validation errors at each
   step and to track them
3) Plot the training and validation errors over the course of model fitting.[^p] 
4) Annotate where you would perform 'early stopping' and compare the 
   computational cost and prediction performance of the 'early stopped' model 
   with the 'fully fitted' version.
   
[^p]: Something like: ![From <akyokus.com>](http://www.akyokus.com/spring2020/ap/lectures/deitel-ipynbs/ch16/ch16images/tensorboard.png)
though you should implement your visualization 'by hand' instead of using a tool
like `TensorBoard`.

## Ridge Regression (9 Points)

Implement ridge regression for both the 'tall' and 'wide' data sets. Use
cross-validation to select an optimal value of $\lambda$. Compare the 
performance against OLS (tall data only) and $K$-nearest neighbors. 

What do you observe? Is this consistent with our discussion of ridge regression
in class? Are your results the same for both data sets or do they differ? 

*You may use `glmnet()` or similar tools for both fitting ridge regression and
for performing cross-validation for this problem.*

## Sparse Regression and Feature Selection (15 Points)

Let us now apply _feature selection_ methods (*i.e.*, LASSO) to the 
wide data set. First, apply lasso regression and use cross-validation to get 
estimates of the prediction error. 

In this problem, you are going to use several strategies to select 'important' 
features. Implement each of the following methods and compare your findings. 
(Note that your results may not be consistent across heuristics - life is hard!)

1. Which are the _first_ variables selected by the lasso? 
2. Which variables are included when you use the "1 standard error" tuning rule?
   How big are their coefficients? 
3. Which variables are included when you use the "minimum error" tuning rule?
   How big are their coefficients? 
4. Which variables are _reliable_ across a range of choices of $\lambda$? 
5. Which variables are selected under a _stability_ analysis? That is, after
   randomly splitting or re-sampling (bootstrapping) the data, which variables
   does a CV-tuned lasso select? If a variable is consistently selected, it is
   more likely to be important than one which is only selected sporadically. 
6. What are the most important variables as indicated by a LOCO study (see the
   previous problem set)? It is computationally expensive to LOCO every variable,
   so I'd recommend doing a LOCO analysis on a somewhat smaller universe of 
   variables, say those that ridge regression assigns the largest coefficients to.
   
Based on your findings, which would you identify as the most important features?
Are these scientifically reasonable?

*As in the previous problem, you may use `glmnet()` or similar tools for both 
fitting the lasso and for performing cross-validation for this problem, but
you need to do the stability, LOCO, *etc* analyses directly rather than using
pre-packaged functionality.*

## Non-Linear Methods (10 Points)

Apply a non-linear regression method to the tall data set, allowing for 
non-linear relationships in any variable where it may make sense. 

1) Use some sort of data-driven tuning to select which variables should be 
   'non-linear' and which should be linear. This can be a simple CV-scheme
   (checking for a statistically significant improvement in prediction by
   'non-linearizing' a feature) or something more advanced. 
2) Visualize and interpret any non-linear relationships in your final model. 

You can use a pre-packaged non-linear model like `mgcv::gam()` or something
more advanced like Sparse Additive Models (SpAM) or trend-fildering if you're
feeling ambitious.
